Slides (black), the lecture notes (green — study guide written from Dr. Alnasser's lecture by Mohammed Alessa, Mohammed Alsalamah & Abdulrahman Alomar) and every gift (red). Aldughaither has no chapter for this lecture.

Outline

  • Pneumothorax · pleural effusion · chest-tube insertion technique · understanding the water-seal drainage system · chest-tube removal technique.

1. Pneumothorax

  • Collection of free air between the parietal and visceral pleura that causes partial or complete collapse of the lung.
Air from outsideAir from inside
TraumaIdiopathic
ThoracocentesisCOPD
Image-guided biopsyPositive-pressure ventilation
Insertion of a venous catheterInfection, tumour, foreign body
Rupture of the oesophagus
TypeAetiology (slide table)
Primary spontaneous (PSP)No underlying lung disease (but blebs/bullae commonly present)
Secondary spontaneous (SSP)Underlying lung disease — COPD, cystic fibrosis, AIDS with emphysema
Traumatic / iatrogenicTrauma to the thorax; secondary to transthoracic or transbronchial lung biopsy (~10%), central venous catheterization, supraclavicular nerve block
  • Primary spontaneous pneumothorax: rupture of a cyst or small sac (bleb) on the surface of the lung.

Apical blebs — rupture of a subpleural bleb; thoracoscopic view

  • Young boy with no lung disease, pneumothorax after the gym → primary spontaneous pneumothorax. 441

Diagnosis — clinical criteria and chest X-ray

  • P-THORAX: Pleuritic chest pain · Tracheal deviation · Hyper-resonance on percussion · Onset sudden · Reduced breath sounds unilaterally · Absent fremitus · X-ray shows lung collapse.
  • X-ray: upright inspiratory chest X-ray — visible pleural edge with no lung markings between it and the chest wall · shrunken lobe or lung · tracheal deviation and mediastinal shift occur with large pneumothoraces.

Chest X-rays — visible pleural line (arrow), absent lung markings, collapsed lung

Therapy — depends on the size

  • Small: O₂ · close observation · needle aspiration of the air.
  • Moderate or large / symptomatic: chest-tube drainage.

Chest drains — small-bore drain with valve, drain in place, collection device; X-ray after drainage

  • Tall, thin 20-year-old, stable, small apical pneumothorax without shift → high-flow oxygen and observation. 442 ×2

2. Tension pneumothorax

  • Life-threatening — requires immediate intervention.
  • Causes: penetrating chest injuries, fractures of the trachea or bronchi, a ruptured oesophagus.
  • Progressive pressure build-up pushes the mediastinum to the opposite hemithorax → obstructs venous return → circulatory instability → cardiac arrest.
  • Patient is tachycardic, tachypnoeic, may be hypoxic; followed by circulatory collapse with hypotension and traumatic arrest with PEA.
  • Diagnosis is always clinical.
  • X-ray (if ever seen): trachea deviated away from the side of the tension · mediastinal shift · depressed hemidiaphragm.

Tension pneumothorax — mediastinal displacement to the opposite side reduces cardiac output; X-ray

Tension PTX therapy

  • Don't forget: life-threatening condition!
  • Emergent chest decompression with needle thoracostomy: a 14–16G IV cannula inserted into the 2nd rib space, mid-clavicular line, advanced until air can be aspirated into an attached syringe.
  • Later: constant tube drainage.

Needle decompression — insert the needle into the 2nd intercostal space over the 3rd rib

  • Trachea deviated to the LEFT, hyper-resonance and absent breath sounds on the RIGHT → needle decompression, 2nd ICS midclavicular line, RIGHT side (no CXR first). 442 ×18
  • During management of tension pneumothorax, the irrelevant step → confirming the chest tube with CT. 438

Recurrent pneumothorax — blebectomy and pleurodesis

Thoracoscopic (VATS) view of apical blebs and stapled blebectomy

Added explanationSurgery (VATS bullectomy/blebectomy + pleurodesis) is offered for a second (recurrent) episode, a persistent air leak or failure to re-expand (> 3–5 days), bilateral or tension pneumothorax, or high-risk occupations (pilots, divers).
  • Second episode of pneumothorax (previous chest tube), now on a chest tube again → VATS bullectomy and pleurodesis. 439
  • Large spontaneous pneumothorax, chest tube in, lung fails to re-expand with a persistent air leak, stable → added key bronchoscopy (this year's thoracic notes: suspect an airway injury; a bigger or extra tube won't fix it). 442

3. Subcutaneous emphysema

  • Air trapped under the skin — a crackling feeling on palpation (subcutaneous crepitation, like touching Rice Krispies).
  • Both penetrating and blunt trauma to the respiratory and GI tracts can cause it.
  • Air forced into the interstitial tissue around the pulmonary vessels travels back to the hilum → pneumomediastinum → neck, face and chest wall.
  • If severe, it can compress the upper airway and jugular veins → airway and cardiovascular compromise; dysphonia and dysphagia as air dissects the neck; rarely progressive dyspnoea needs tracheostomy.

Crepitus on palpation — "Rice Krispies"

Massive subcutaneous emphysema of the face and trunk ("Michelin man")

CT and X-ray — air in the soft tissues

Management

  • Control the source!
  • Be sure about the tube position / holes · the patency of the tube · the water-seal system.
  • Techniques from case reports: bilateral 3-cm infraclavicular incisions down to the pectoralis fascia · a drain/chest tube used as a subcutaneous drain on gentle suction · a modified microcatheter with compressive massage toward it.

Subcutaneous fenestrated drains and negative-pressure wound therapy for subcutaneous emphysema

4. Pleural effusion

  • Accumulation of fluid between the parietal and visceral pleura. Pleural fluid is normally made in small amounts to lubricate the pleura; an effusion is an abnormal collection.
  • Pathophysiology: ↑ pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (CHF) · ↓ oncotic pressure (low serum albumin) · ↓ pleural-space pressure (lung collapse) · ↑ microvascular permeability (inflammatory mediators) · impaired lymphatic drainage (tumour/fibrosis) · occlusion of parietal-pleura stomata (inflammation, malignancy).
  • Symptoms: chest pain, dyspnoea, cough. Exam: percussion dull; breath sounds diminished/absent.
  • X-ray: small effusion → blunting of the costophrenic angle; large → homogeneous opacity.

Effusion on X-ray — costophrenic blunting; large homogeneous effusion

Thoracocentesis

  • A procedure to remove fluid from the pleural cavity.
  • Risks: pneumothorax, fluid re-accumulation, pulmonary oedema (re-expansion), bleeding, infection, respiratory distress.

Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis — insert the needle above the rib

Analysis

  • Quantity · quality (colour, density, opacity) · lab analysis — chemical, cytological, microbiological.

Fluid LDH / serum LDH≤ 0.6> 0.6
Fluid LDH≤ ⅔ upper limit of normal serum LDH> ⅔ upper limit

5. Empyema

  • Pus in the pleural space. Bacteria: Strep. pneumoniae, Staph. aureus, Klebsiella, E. coli, M. tuberculosis, anaerobes.
  • Risk factors: alcoholism, drug use, HIV, neoplasm, pre-existing lung disease.
  • Complication of bacterial pneumonia, subdiaphragmatic abscess, oesophageal perforation, thoracic surgery.
  • Symptoms: chest pain, dyspnoea, cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss.
  • Diagnosis: X-ray (pleural fluid) · ultrasound · CT · thoracocentesis: pus!
  • Therapy: prompt chest-tube drainage + broad-spectrum antibiotics; ineffective therapy, recurrence or pleural thickening (functional lung impairment) → surgical decortication.

Empyema — CT (split-pleura sign), aspirated pus, loculated collections

StageImagingTreatment
I — exudativeNo loculationsDrainage (thoracentesis or chest tube) + antibiotics
II — fibrinopurulentLoculationsFibrinolytic therapy (thoracoscopy for failures) + antibiotics
III — organizingFibrous peelLikely thoracotomy/decortication (thoracoscopy in selected patients) + antibiotics

Empyema stages and time scale — drainage (weeks 0–2), fibrinolysis/VATS (to ~5 weeks), decortication / open-window thoracostomy / thoracoplasty later

  • Intrapleural t-PA + DNase (MIST-2 trial): t-PA 10 mg + DNase 5 mg, twice daily for 3 days, clamping the drain for 1 hour after each dose → better drainage, fewer surgical referrals, shorter stay (each drug alone did not help).

VATS and open decortication — removing the fibrous peel

6. Chest tubes

  • Small bore (12–20 Fr) · large bore (24–32 Fr).

Small-bore (pigtail) and large-bore chest tubes

Chest drainage units (Atrium)

Indications

  • Pneumothorax (trauma, lung disease, procedure complications).
  • Haemothorax (blunt or penetrating trauma).
  • Haemopneumothorax.
  • Tension pneumothorax — injured tissue forms a one-way valve (emergency).
  • Pleural effusion · empyema · chylothorax — lymph in the pleura (trauma, tumour, mediastinal surgery) → milky white fluid.
  • Not an indication for a chest tube → pneumoperitoneum. 437
  • After oesophagectomy, drain fluid that turns milky white after oral intake → thoracic duct injury (chylothorax). 439 ×2

Insertion site

  • Superior direction → removal of air (pneumothorax); inferior direction → removal of fluid (haemothorax, empyema); posterior placement for loculated fluid/air — image-guided only.
  • Safe triangle — minimizes injury to the internal mammary artery, muscle or breast tissue. All experts agree: a tube in the midaxillary line between the 4th and 5th ribs drains fluid or vents air.

The safe triangle — lateral edge of pectoralis major, anterior edge of latissimus dorsi, nipple line (5th ICS)

  • Safe triangle: anterior border pectoralis major, posterior border latissimus dorsi, inferior limit ≈ nipple / 5th ICS line; entry 4th–5th ICS, mid-axillary line, just above the rib. Staying inside it avoids abdominal/diaphragmatic injury (too low) and needless muscle trauma (less pain).
  • Ideal chest-tube location → 4th intercostal space above the 5th rib, mid-axillary line. 439 ×9

Instruments

  • Simple thoracostomy kit: povidone–iodine/ChloraPrep, sterile towels and drapes, sponges, 2 Kelly clamps, 1% lidocaine without epinephrine (40–50 mL), non-absorbable suture, 18/21/25G needles, needle holder, scalpel (#10), scissors, 10 mL syringe, sterile gown, gloves, mask and cap, gauze, chest tube and drainage system, vented chest seals, marker.

Chest-tube insertion kit

  • When inserting a chest tube → full aseptic technique (no CT, no GA; adult trauma tubes are large-bore, not 12–14 Fr). 436

Technique

  • Identify the site: 4th or 5th ICS, anterior axillary line (or between anterior and mid-axillary lines) — the safe zone; mark and clean.
  • Incise tissue to the depth of the rib → carefully confirm depth and location → bluntly dissect the intercostal muscle and carefully insert a finger → ensure entry into the pleural cavity and remove adhesions if present → remove the finger, insert the tube and monitor the patient.

Marking the 4th–5th intercostal space in the safe zone

Incise to the depth of the rib; confirm depth and location

Blunt dissection over the rib, finger sweep into the pleural cavity, tract ready for the tube

  • Infiltrate local anaesthetic through every layer, not just the skin; re-infiltrate at the intercostals. Confirm the pleural space with a finger before advancing the tube (ultrasound helps localize, but the finger check is still needed). Don't force through adhesions — slow down, ask for help; a thick pleura may be safer in the OR.

7. The chest-tube system

  • 3-bottle system: patient → collection bottle → water-seal bottle → suction-control bottle → suction.

The three-bottle system

  • Collection chamber: collects drainage. Water seal: maintained at 2 cm — a one-way valve that prevents air or fluid returning to the chest.

Collection bottle and water seal

  • Suction control: the straw submerged in the suction-control bottle (typically 20 cmH₂O) limits the negative pressure applied to the pleura (−20 cmH₂O); it is open to the atmosphere, so as the vacuum rises bubbling begins (air is drawn in to limit suction).
  • The depth of water in the suction bottle — NOT the reading on the vacuum regulator — determines the negative pressure transmitted to the chest. Higher negative pressure increases flow but can damage lung tissue.

Suction control — the depth of the straw sets the suction

Modern drainage unit (Atrium)

  • A: collection chamber · B: water seal · C: suction control.
  • Collection chamber: fluid drains via a 6-ft patient tube; calibrated in mL; write on the surface the level, date and time.
  • Water seal: prevents air re-entering · intrathoracic pressure monitoring · a float valve protects against high negativity from stripping/milking. Ensure 2 cmH₂O. Normal: "tidaling" with breathing. Abnormal: bubbling = air leak → check connections and the dressing site for a withdrawn catheter; find the source by briefly clamping the patient tube and seeing whether the bubbling stops.
  • Suction control: dry suction — set the rotary dial (e.g. −20 cmH₂O), wall suction to −40 mmHg; the orange bellows expand to the delta mark when working. Wet suction — fill to the prescribed level (−20 cmH₂O), ensure gentle bubbling.

Modern chest-drain units

Atrium unit — collection chamber, water seal, suction control

Dry vs wet suction control

  • Heimlich (flutter) valve: one-way valve that lets air escape but not re-enter · for a small or partial pneumothorax · does not collect fluid · the inner valve moves on exhalation · for stable patients — more mobility.

Heimlich flutter valve

Portable drainage devices

  • Setting up: fill the water-seal chamber with 2 cm of sterile water (turns blue) → connect the patient tube → set up suction (water suction: fill to 20 cm, connect and increase the vacuum until gentle bubbling; dry suction: set the dial, connect, wall suction −40 mmHg or higher).

Setting up the system

  • Suction adds negative pressure so drainage exceeds gravity alone. If −20 is prescribed, the drainage system (water column or dry regulator) sets the pressure — not the wall dial. Wet = older, gentle bubbling; dry = the lecturer's preferred system (settings −10/−20/−30/−40 cmH₂O, portable versions).
  • Suction is NOT routine — most patients stay on water seal. Two exceptions: after decortication and after surgery for spontaneous pneumothorax — to keep the lung apposed to the chest wall and close the residual space.

8. Assessment

  • What to find out: is the tube in place / kinked? Drainage in the last 24 h? Nature of the fluid? Air leak — how much, inspiratory/expiratory/both? Subcutaneous emphysema? On suction — how much? Look at the CXR every day.
  • STOP: Site · Tubing · Output · Patency.
  • S = Site: tube in place · no signs of infection · dressing changed every 48 h and when wet/soiled (sterile technique) · subcutaneous emphysema (palpate for crepitus).

Checking the insertion site and dressing; palpating for crepitus

  • T = Tubing: connections secured · no kinks · keep the drainage system below the patient's level.
  • O = Output: document amount, type and colour; mark the chamber with date and time.

Tubing and output

  • P = Patency — A: water seal (check with the suction off): too high → harder for air to leave (aspirate water); too low → air exposure → pneumothorax (add sterile water).
  • P — B: bubbling = a leak unless the patient has a pneumothorax: intermittent → air leak from the pleura (resolves as the lung re-expands); continuous → leak in the system.
  • P — C: fluctuations: normal water-seal level −10 cm on inspiration, −4 cm on expiration; if fluctuations stop, the tubing may be obstructed (kinks, patient lying on it). > 2 cm water → drainage decreases; < 2 cm → risk of pneumothorax.
  • Rounds checklist: on suction or water seal? Recent output (e.g. last 3 h), not just the total · mark the level at a fixed time (e.g. 6 AM) · fluid character · air-leak pattern.

At the bedside

  • Always keep the drain BELOW the chest — gravity drainage (higher pressure in the chest → fluid moves to lower pressure).
  • Emergency actions: tube dislodged from the device → clamp it or put the end in a bottle of sterile water (one-way valve), prepare a new device, reconnect · tube pulled out of the patient → cover the site with Vaseline gauze at peak inspiration, call for help.

Drain below the chest · covering the insertion site

Clamping

  • Clamp only when: changing the drainage device · checking for an air leak · tubing disconnected and sterile water out of reach · checking lung re-expansion before removal.
  • Do NOT clamp when ambulating or for transport (disconnect suction at the suction-control stopcock instead).
  • Clamp trial (exam point): if unsure the patient is ready for removal (equivocal air leak) → clamp ~5–6 h, then CXR; a recurrent pneumothorax = persistent leak.

9. Chest-tube removal

  • Indications: improved respiratory status · symmetrical chest movement · bilateral breath sounds · decreased drainage · no bubbling in the water seal during inspiration · improved CXR.
  • Process: premedicate for pain · deep exhalation/inspiration practice · sterile supplies · lateral decubitus position · patient performs a Valsalva manoeuvre while the tube is removed · occlusive dressing · post-removal CXR to confirm the lung stays inflated.

10. Complications

PhaseComplications
PlacementDamage to vital structures (lung, heart, liver, spleen) · haemorrhage (great vessels, heart, intercostal artery) · neurological damage (phrenic nerve) · chylothorax
MaintenanceRe-expansion pulmonary oedema · subcutaneous emphysema · lung entrapment · pneumothorax from inadvertent disconnection · empyema
DiscontinuationRecurrence of pneumothorax · pleurocutaneous fistula

CT and autopsy images — chest tubes misplaced into the liver/abdomen and through the lung

Related trauma questions (filed under chest tube)

  • Haemothorax draining 1800 mL immediately → urgent thoracotomy. 442 ×3
  • Stab wound right chest, BP 80/40, GCS 15 → chest tube insertion. 439 ×8
  • Gunshot with a sucking chest wound, BP 70/30 → keyed three-sided dressing. 434 ×3

Mastery checklist (notes)

  • Safe triangle = pectoralis major (anterior) + latissimus dorsi (posterior) + nipple/5th ICS line (inferior); enter the 4th–5th ICS, mid-axillary, above the rib.
  • Anaesthetize every layer and confirm the pleural space with a finger before advancing the tube.
  • Adhesions/thick pleura → don't force dissection; consider the OR.
  • Water seal (~2 cm) lets air out but blocks backflow; suction boosts drainage beyond gravity.
  • Effective suction is set by the drainage system, not by the wall dial.
  • Wet suction → gentle bubbling; dry suction (lecturer's preference) → bellows, −10/−20/−30/−40 cmH₂O.
  • Rounds: connection, recent drainage, fixed-time marking, fluid character, air-leak pattern.
  • Don't clamp routinely; clamp trial (5–6 h then CXR) when readiness for removal is uncertain.
  • Suction only after decortication or surgery for spontaneous pneumothorax.
